utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, the gentleman from the Defence is saying that he's asking his last question, and this is, I think, the 10th time he's asking his last question. Could I hear that last question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During your service with the Armija of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zenica, did you work for the press office of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I never worked for the press office, because I have no propensity for it. But I could know -- I had ways of knowing what they did in the press office, but I paid no attention to it. There are, however, some articles of mine which can be found in the then press. But one thing that I wish to say. I don't really know if the first accused is here. Between 1991 and this day, I never mentioned his name. This is the first time I come across his name in the company. He is, to me, a non-existent person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, is there anything you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I think the Defence of Mr. Kordic took all the questions which we had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you still have in front of you, just so we can deal with it now, Z65, the police report? Do you have that document in front of you, Mr. Cicak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked several questions about it, but just one thing arising from the last question you were asked about names. Will you look, please, to the third paragraph from the end?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second page, third paragraph from the end of the document, third substantial paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the English version, that reads as follows: "I can say that on the following day, I went to see Ivan Kordic, HDZ president in Busovaca, and asked him that the money and other things taken by those six be returned to me and why he had ordered it to be done to me." Then will you come back, please, to the first page, and it's looking at substantial paragraphs -- the fourth substantial paragraph, where you name the people, and you say that, "I know two by their names and surnames, Dario Brnada from Putis and Marko Kulic from Bare, both from Busovaca." Then the report goes on to say, "The others are also from Busovaca and are members of the paramilitary formation of the HDZ reserve service of Herceg-Bosna." There is then a colon, and the names are set out, including Dario Kordic, Sliskovic and Prusac. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you telling the police that Kordic had been one of the people who had attacked you, or were you telling him that you had asked Kordic why he had ordered it to be done to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object to that question, Your Honour, on the ground that this document speaks for itself, and it's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is entitled to interpret what it was that he was saying in the document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to read the document carefully once again. It says here that I know Dario Brnada from Putis and Marko Kulic, as we call him Zelenika from Bare, both from Busovaca, and the others also from Busovaca, and there should simply be a full stop there. On the left-hand side was also a man with a small beard, and that beard was worn by Svabo. Then the sentence goes on, "members of the paramilitary formation of the HDZ reserve service," that is to say held by Kordic. So I did not say that it was Kordic who had beaten me, but these were members of the paramilitary formation that are kept by Dario Kordic, Anto and Franjo Sliskovic and Igor Prusac. I think that is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm sorry to intervene. The witness, Cicak, gave his opinion, and he read part of this. However, he added a part that does not exist over here, the part about the man with a beard. That is not mentioned here in this criminal report. That is why I had to intervene.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, I have to say that you did not listen to me carefully. I said this yesterday, not today. Please be attentive and listen to what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. It won't assist for you to abuse Defence counsel. There's a matter I should have raised with Mr. Sayers. It's this: Is there any dispute that this witness was beaten up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't see how there could be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it, then, the answer is, "No, it's not disputed."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think it's disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then the next point is this: Is there any dispute that the witness complained to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know, Your Honour, in all candour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kordic will know. It may not be the terms of the complaint, but in general terms, is there any argument that this witness complained about being beaten up to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that there was a meeting, that he complained about having been beaten by persons unknown, and I also believe that he showed the bruises that the photographs showed on his body. The other versions of events that this witness has given today and in the earlier days, I believe, are completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there may be dispute about the details, but the outline appears not to be in dispute. Yes, Mr. Nice, I hope you can finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, certainly. I've only got --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've only got about half a dozen topics, or perhaps eight. And I've only got one more, I think, on a document that I want the witness to look at, so perhaps we can deal with that now. 64,2 and 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, if you look at this, remind yourself what it is. It's a newspaper article for which we have a part translation. If you look at the two second sheets where there is a small block of type in relation -- on each page, or, no, there's one page with a small block of type, that part of the newspaper article reflects your being asked questions by a reporter and your answering those questions. If the Court would be good enough to look at the English version pretty well dead centre of the block of type. You were asked yesterday about not telling the investigators of your account that when you went to see Kordic after the beating, he told you that he expected you to come repenting, not complaining. Is it right that you said that to the newspaper reporter, when you were asked questions about this attack immediately afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Did I say this? Yes, yes, it's true. But I told Kordic that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That can go back. Your Honour, there's one slightly technical point. I should deal with it before the witness leaves the stand. It relates to Defence Exhibit D9/1. This was a document provided to you in B/C/S/ with an English translation, following on documentation provided by the Prosecution to the Defence. You will recall the document, for you yourself observed that there was a question mark beside a date. If you possibly remember it, you observed. The position is that the English translation provided by the Defence may, in reality, be somewhat inappropriate for this reason: The documents provided, which were, in fact, in excess of our duties and, in a sense, by oversight, are investigators' notes rather than an interview. They are not a signed document at all. This all happened a long time ago, way before I knew anything about any of these matters. But I think the original document was maybe hand-written but in English, was typed up in English, and the B/C/S/ that was provided pursuant to our obligations, we having provided the document in English, is a translation into B/C/S/. There is therefore no need to re-translate it back. That's not helpful. What you will need to have, at some stage, would be the original typed up English notes of the investigator, which indeed explain why there are question marks present on the document. They are Exhibit 2704 in the Prosecution numbering of exhibits, but it may be that you would rather keep them associated with the Defence exhibit, the number of which I've just given you. Hand those in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be most convenient if they go into the Defence exhibits as D9/1(a).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. But unless there's any -- I've explained the position. I don't imagine it's controversial, and I'm not going to ask the witness anything further about it. The following couple of questions -- and I don't desire the witness to look at it, as I've explained. He doesn't need to look at it. It was dealing with something at an appropriate stage. So the usher can take the document away, and we'll move on to the next two questions, which can probably be answered, Mr. Cicak, simply by a "Yes" or a "No".

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In relation to a medical certificate that you've been asked about, did you have a copy of that at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here's the original. You have the copy with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no. This is the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So did you have a copy -- please listen to me, Mr. Cicak, because it will make life easier for you. Were you provided with a copy at the time of your examination, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: During my examination by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the doctor.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what the procedure at doctors' examinations is here, but doctors usually write this down immediately, directly, whatever they see and ascertain. When he puts all the papers together, then he writes a --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to withdraw that question. I'm going to move on. Mr. Cicak, I'm going to turn to another topic, please. Guns. In the course of this history -- forget your sporting gun. In the course of this history, did you receive a gun of any kind, yourself, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not receive a gun. I received a pistol, as a member of the narrow leadership of the HDZ, and it was free of charge, at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who provided you with that gun?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was at a faraway place, at a man called Tunjo. His real name is Anto Arapovic, I think, but his nickname is Tunjo. He's a local person, and he's a land surveyor, and his house is on the outskirts of the town of Busovaca itself, and we had a meeting there. I believe that Anto Sliskovic was there, and Anto Bilic and others, and Mr. Kordic, and I was given a pistol or whatever you call it, a very heavy one. It was not usable, as far as I was concerned, at all, nor would I have ever used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Picking up on something you were asked by Judge Bennouna, in the period 1991 and 1992, how widely or otherwise did you travel in the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And '92.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as necessary, but I think I travelled a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you went to other locations, did you meet members of the HDZ in those locations sometimes, frequently, never, rarely; what was the position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you discuss current political matters with them or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It depends on the nature of the meeting concerned. If it was official, then I discussed it, and if it was a private journey, then we would do something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We know what your views were, and there's no need to repeat them, but please tell the Tribunal this: Insofar as you did discuss views with other people in the HDZ when you met them, were your views -- did they receive any support, were they entirely eccentric, did they receive a majority of support? Tell us, but again, briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: My views were received remarkably well, and no one ever opposed them, except at the time when I went through a total collapse, physical and psychological, when I was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That brings me to this next question on the same topic. You, as we know, were publishing articles, expressing views in very strong terms. Were you the only person expressing such views publicly, or were others doing the same thing, or were lots of people doing the same thing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that many persons presented such views, but I was the only one from the HDZ who presented this. However, other citizens also agreed, or rather presented their views, which were very, very close to my own perceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about Busovaca being but one of 70 or, as you would say, a hundred municipalities, and therefore your lowly position in the overall hierarchy of the party. We know that Travnik was one of several regions. Did all regions and municipalities have the same degree of authority and importance or did they have different importance and significance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: They had different degrees. One can say that this was a total disorganisation in the party. There were some municipalities where there was only a president, where there wasn't even a board, a committee, nothing. The Travnik region or the town of Busovaca were amongst the more organised municipalities of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that the first defendant, Kordic, ceased to be the president of the Busovaca party on the 1st of April of 1992, and you appeared to accept that. First of all, do you know, in the sense that you know from some source, that he did cease to be the president on that day, the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that the date is wrong. Mr. Glavocevic did not take over this office from Dario Kordic on that day but later. I have that particular figure. But should I look it up, should I tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't trouble. You're saying you think it's later. It may not matter. But this question, please help me. You became aware of his giving up that office, or losing that office, or whatever it may be. So far you could judge, did that change the position of him in relation to local affairs? Did that change his authority at all? What was the position, so far as you could judge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is an excellent question that you've put. Of course, it should have been put earlier on. The political, military and civilian government and authorities, or rather the administrative authorities at that time, were totally undivided. Whoever was in power, regardless of where he was, whether he was the president of the HDZ, regardless of whether he was commander, regardless of whether he was president of the municipality, he was a powerful person, and whatever he said was carried out by all who were supposed to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in power at the time that you're talking about, that is, before and after any resignation or dismissal of Kordic from the position of president of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only one word should be said before that, and that is that Busovaca became too small for Kordic, for his ambitions and his development, and therefore he had to reach an agreement with the municipal board of the HDZ that he should leave that office, that he should move further on, because he had aspired for the top echelons of the HDZ. Mr. Glavocevic assumed this duty, and later on I found out that he had major difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think my last question is this: It was put to you in a question that may have been in two parts, that Mr. Udovicic, himself, proposed the move of the Travnik regional party to Busovaca, and you may have appeared to have accepted that proposition, that he proposed it himself. Just help us. Did Mr. Udovicic propose that move or not, or can't you remember, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my modest opinion, Mr. Udovicic would never have proposed anything that stupid. It is a well-known thing, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that Travnik is a city with a long tradition, the city of viziers. That it be moved from that town to a village, that is to say to Busovaca, for Busovaca to become the centre, possibly somebody else could have proposed it and then it was accepted by others at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that concludes all I want to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, it may not matter very much, but you were asked what age you retired. Would you like to tell us, or do you have some objection to telling us that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: You are really putting me into an embarrassing position. Now I have to try to make -- to do all the math right, how old I was when I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Cicak, let us leave aside your personal situation. The question was put to you, and I believe that you answered that there was a legal age at which you would go and retire. So this applies to everybody, doesn't it, in the country you belong to? There is an age at which people retire, and that happens in all countries in the world. So could you tell us, what is the legal age for retirement in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there where you were? You said that there was a rule or a law applying there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there is. There is a limit, that is to say that you can retire after 35 years of service or when you reach the age of 55. That's the way it was then. I retired a bit earlier, so my pension was 1,5 per cent lower than it would have been otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cicak. You are now released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now free to go home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I say something, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the last time, and provided it's brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that you can allow me to do so because I am going home. It is the first time in my life that I was told that I was lying, and I never would have expected that from the gentleman of the Defence. If I had been beaten up, if I had been beaten black and blue, I mean, for someone to bring this into question, that is beyond my imagination. I would like to thank you for everything you have done for me here. I felt all right, and I believe that I have contributed as much as I could have. There is one more thing I wish to say, that there are quite a few more documents that have remained unclarified, but you will be the best judge of that. I have some papers with me that speak about certain events, and the gentleman had the right to raise these questions, but he didn't. Regrettably, I shall go home deprived of having been given the possibility to give an answer to these questions, and these questions are very important for me, but thank you for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since you have finished your evidence, Mr. Cicak, if you want to talk to the Prosecution about those documents, you can. No doubt Mr. Nice will speak to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I detain you for a couple of minutes? Nothing to do with this witness, usual problems, but it's better dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No more than two minutes. Thank you, Mr. Cicak. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the organisation of witnesses, which is one of the major problems we face here, as of course you know. I explained the position yesterday, and I got it wrong, actually. The critical witness whose timetable is so inflexible, for understandable reasons, comes in on Monday and won't be available till Tuesday, and I don't know if I can accelerate him to be available on Monday. The witness who will start tomorrow will last, I would have thought, about a day, but of course so far one's estimates have been underestimates. He may last longer, and with cross-examination, he could find himself taken into next Monday afternoon in any event, although that would mean over a day and a half. Possible, but I have plans to try and make his evidence compact, which might make that improbable. Next component is Victims and Witness Unit apparently don't have a precedent for taking a witness back home midway through evidence and viewed the issue as one that was somewhat surprising. They do need to know by 4.30 today whether the second witness, because it's the second witness I am referring to, who we were otherwise going to have for a bit of his evidence in chief, they need to know by 4.30 today whether he is to leave tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Shall we make every effort to ensure that the witness who you are going to call tomorrow morning is finished by 12.30 on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would seem to be the most sensible course, in which you can assist as much as anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly intend to. As to the other witness, if I send him home, which I think is really the proper course, and if I can't get the other witness or any other witness here, which is improbable, for Monday, that would mean that the two hours of Court sitting allocated for Monday afternoon would be abandoned, unless there were an issue we could properly argue. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We think the witness should go. There is an argument to be heard about the admissibility of evidence relating to the search warrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We might be able to tee that up for Monday afternoon. Perhaps I can discuss that with my friends opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and let us know in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. The only other quick point -- I've exceeded my two minutes -- is this: The translation of documents order is about to reach its expiry date -- well, a couple of weeks' time. There are two documents, both extensive, one in Swedish and one in Spanish, for which we have no in-house interpreters. Translation of such documents are farmed out and subcontracted. It takes time, and of course it's very costly. I have asked my friends opposite to consider those documents -- they have had them in their original languages already -- and to let me know whether they do require them to be translated, or alternatively, since these are not witnesses who will be coming immediately, whether we can, in respect of those documents, seek a waiver from the order and put things on hold so as not simply to run the risk of wasting money. If we are able to agree a waiver amongst ourselves, I hope that will be acceptable to the Chamber; if not, can I bring the matter back to you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I hope agreement can be reached. It seems a sensible course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. 9.45 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of April, 1999, at 9.45 a.m.
